primary_cause: Most likely macro-led selloff in cyclical semis/capex-sensitive names not a discrete AMAT headline. No clear AMAT-specific Reuters item in April 12-15
secondary_factors: General concern that chip-equipment demand would weaken if the COVID shock crushed electronics and industrial capex
store_description: With no strong AMAT-specific catalyst the 4.0% drop looks most consistent with a broad de-risking move after March retail sales fell 8.7%. Equipment makers were especially vulnerable because investors were repricing future semiconductor capital spending.

primary_cause: Macro/sector weakness in semis and cyclicals rather than a fresh Broadcom headline. No compelling Broadcom-specific Reuters catalyst in April 12-15
secondary_factors: Investor concern about enterprise handset and infrastructure demand during the COVID shutdown
store_description: AVGO's 3.8% decline appears to have been part of the same April 15 risk-off trade that hit other growth-cyclicals after recession alarms and terrible March data. Without a stock-specific headline the best explanation is investors discounting weaker end-market demand.

primary_cause: Financial-sector credit-loss/recession repricing with AXP hit because it is both a payments company and a lender exposed to consumer/travel spending
secondary_factors: Travel and entertainment volumes collapsing during lockdowns which was especially relevant for AmEx's revenue mix
store_description: AXP's 5.2% drop fits a period when investors were reassessing lenders and card issuers after banks began posting multibillion-dollar reserve builds against a coming recession with travel spending effectively frozen and consumer credit risk rising.

primary_cause: Own earnings release and recession warning. On April 15 Bank of America reported Q1 profit fell 48.5% and set aside $3.6 billion for potential loan losses
secondary_factors: Sector-wide fear over loan-loss reserving and concern that the true credit damage had not yet shown up
store_description: BAC's drop was highly company-specific. The bank disclosed a 48.5% plunge in quarterly net income and a $3.6 billion reserve build explicitly warning that it expected a recession because of COVID-19.

primary_cause: Financial-sector contagion from bank earnings and recession fears. No major negative BK-specific Reuters headline on April 12-15
secondary_factors: Custody banks sensitive to falling asset values lower rates and fears around capital-markets activity and fee income
store_description: No decisive BK-specific event in the 3-day window. The 4.7% fall is best explained by read-through from other banks' earnings collapsing rate expectations and concern that market turmoil would pressure both fee revenue and balance-sheet earnings.

primary_cause: Retail/cyclical macro shock not a discrete HD announcement. Main relevant news was the record 8.7% March retail sales drop
secondary_factors: Concern that lockdowns and job losses would hit big-ticket home-improvement demand
store_description: HD's 4.2% drop appears to have been driven by the ugly macro print more than company news. When investors saw March retail sales down 8.7% they sold economically sensitive consumer names broadly including home improvement.

primary_cause: Own earnings release with large credit-loss reserve build. On April 15 Citigroup said Q1 profit fell 46% after setting aside nearly $5 billion for expected loan defaults
secondary_factors: Terrible macro data and broader investor concern that actual charge-offs were still ahead
store_description: Citi's drop was strongly stock-specific. The bank reported profit down 46% and built almost $5 billion of reserves for a likely wave of defaults confirming how quickly the pandemic recession was changing bank balance-sheet assumptions.

primary_cause: Continuation of industrial/recession and capex fears. Caterpillar withdrew 2020 guidance on March 26 and suspended some operations because of COVID uncertainty
secondary_factors: Weak industrial production data and concern about energy mining and construction demand
store_description: CAT had already told investors it was withdrawing guidance and suspending operations because of pandemic disruption. By April 15 another round of awful macro data reinforced the view that heavy-equipment demand would be weak across construction mining and energy end markets.

primary_cause: Pre-earnings weakness tied to expected AUM/earnings pressure from market turmoil. BlackRock's Q1 report came April 16 showing net income fell to $806 million from $1.05 billion
secondary_factors: Broad financial-sector weakness and recession fears
store_description: BLK's 3.3% fall likely reflected caution ahead of next-day results in a period of violent market moves. When BlackRock reported profits were down and flows were skewing toward cash and defensive positioning validating the market's caution.

primary_cause: Read-through from banks' credit-loss provisions to consumer lenders. No COF-specific Reuters item in the window but Capital One is one of the more recession-sensitive consumer lenders
secondary_factors: COF's exposure to credit cards and consumer credit made it especially vulnerable as unemployment surged
store_description: Even without a fresh COF headline the stock's 5.0% drop makes sense with BAC and Citi having just shown massive reserve builds and investors extrapolating that pain to consumer lenders with more unsecured exposure.

primary_cause: Crude-price weakness and renewed doubt that supply cuts could offset demand destruction. Reuters said U.S. crude slid back toward $20 per barrel on April 14
secondary_factors: Continued fear that producers would need more capex cuts and that 2020 cash flows would collapse
store_description: COP's 5.5% decline was fundamentally an oil move. Reuters reported WTI sliding back toward $20 as traders concluded that record producer cuts were still playing catch-up to catastrophic demand destruction from COVID shutdowns.

primary_cause: Defensive-sector selloff tied to recession worries and reduced power-demand expectations rather than a fresh company event
secondary_factors: Utilities also affected by lower rates and broad portfolio reshuffling after the sharp rally in defensives earlier in the crisis
store_description: DUK's 3.2% decline appears to have been a macro move not an idiosyncratic one. As investors absorbed recession warnings even utilities got hit on concern that commercial and industrial power demand would soften materially.

primary_cause: Macro-led selloff in industrials exposed to capex and factory activity. No EMR-specific Reuters headline in April 12-15
secondary_factors: Concerns about weaker automation process-control and industrial end-market demand as factory output fell
store_description: EMR fell more than the market because it was leveraged to industrial output and capital spending just as the data deteriorated sharply with March retail sales collapsing 8.7% and industrial activity weakening.

primary_cause: Macro/global-growth fears not a fresh FedEx announcement. No FedEx-specific Reuters headline in April 12-15
secondary_factors: Investors were likely concerned that B2B volumes and international shipping would weaken badly even if consumer parcel demand later improved
store_description: FDX often trades as a real-time economic barometer and on April 15 the barometer looked ugly. With retail factory and recession data deteriorating the market was marking down FedEx on the assumption that high-margin commercial and international package activity would contract sharply.

primary_cause: Broad industrial/aerospace-defense risk-off move not a specific GD catalyst verified. No GD-specific Reuters article in the 3-day window
secondary_factors: Concern about business jet exposure and general program uncertainty during the early COVID shock
store_description: GD's 3.4% decline looks more like sector beta than company news. In mid-April 2020 investors were still selling global cyclicals and capital-goods names as recession estimates worsened and GD fit that risk bucket despite its defense exposure.

primary_cause: Most likely broad market/biotech profit-taking not a verified negative GILD-specific event. No negative remdesivir headline before April 15 and positive remdesivir anecdotes actually hit April 16 after the drop
secondary_factors: Some investors may have rotated out of defensives/healthcare after earlier relative outperformance
store_description: Could not verify a stock-specific negative Gilead development in the three days before the 4.0% drop. Since the notable remdesivir optimism surfaced on April 16 after the decline the move was probably more about general market weakness.

primary_cause: COVID disruption to NBCUniversal's parks film TV production and sports businesses. Universal theme parks had extended closures through at least April 19
secondary_factors: General ad-market pressure and recession fears hurting media valuations
store_description: CMCSA's 3.5% decline had a real business read-through. NBCUniversal's parks were closed through at least April 19 and theme parks sports production and much of film and TV production had been suspended making Comcast more exposed than a plain cable name.

primary_cause: Lagged reaction to JPM's own earnings/recession outlook. On April 14 JPMorgan gave what Reuters called a glum outlook and executives said the worst was still ahead
secondary_factors: Continued selling across banks after BAC and Citi also posted huge reserve builds on April 15
store_description: JPM's April 16 decline looks like a continuation of the negative bank-earnings read-through. Reuters said JPMorgan had offered a grim outlook for the COVID recession and stressed that the worst is yet to come while other banks reinforced the same story.

primary_cause: Oil-price weakness/demand destruction. Reuters reported on April 14 that crude fell sharply as traders judged demand destruction too severe for OPEC+ cuts to offset
secondary_factors: Investor concern about capital spending cuts balance-sheet stress and the possibility the downturn would last longer
store_description: XOM's 3.3% drop on April 16 was still mainly an oil-market story with Reuters reporting WTI sliding back toward $20 per barrel and Exxon having already pledged significant spending cuts as the pandemic crushed fuel demand.

primary_cause: Own earnings release and grim outlook. On April 14 Reuters reported Wells Fargo's first-quarter profit was decimated as it set aside billions for potential loan losses
secondary_factors: Continued pressure after BAC and Citi's April 15 reserve builds reinforced that the entire banking system was bracing for large credit losses
store_description: WFC's 5.5% drop on April 16 was a direct aftershock from its April 14 earnings. Reuters said profit plunged because the bank set aside billions for loan losses and management signaled that the recession would get worse before it got better.
